draft.title: Graphs of polynomials
card: Each factor of a polynomial gives an x-intercept. For \(y = (x + 1)(x - 3)\), the intercepts are at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\).
A single root is from a factor that appears once. The curve crosses the x-axis there.
A double root is from a factor that is squared, such as \((x - 2)^{2}\). The curve touches the x-axis there and turns back.
The y-intercept is found by putting \(x = 0\). For a positive leading coefficient, the right end of the curve goes up.

3.alt: The curve \(y = (x + 1)(x - 2)^{2}\). It crosses the x-axis at \(x = -1\), touches it at \(x = 2\), and crosses the y-axis at \(y = 4\).

draft.remember: A single root crosses the axis. A double root touches it and turns back.

a.q: The curve \(y = (x - 4)^{2}(x + 1)\) meets the x-axis at \(x = 4\). What does the curve do there?
opts: Touches the axis and turns back
a.why: The factor \((x - 4)\) is squared, so \(x = 4\) is a double root and the curve touches the axis and turns back. A crossing happens only at a single root such as \(x = -1\).
a.clue: Look at the power on the factor \((x - 4)\).

b.q: Mia sketches \(y = (x - 1)(x + 3)^{2}\). Where does her curve cross the y-axis?
b.why: Put \(x = 0\): \((0 - 1)(0 + 3)^{2} = -1 \times 9 = -9\). The answer \(9\) comes from forgetting the sign of the factor \((x - 1)\).
b.clue: Substitute \(x = 0\) and keep the sign of each factor.

a.best: Touches the axis and turns back

problems.detail: The why says 'A crossing happens only at a single root'. This is not true in general: a curve also crosses at a root from a cubed factor, such as \((x - 4)^{3}\). The card only says a single root crosses, so the 'only' overstates it. Reword, for example: 'At a single root such as \(x = -1\), the curve crosses instead.'
